rows.summary: Google’s AI-infrastructure thesis strengthens within 5/5 because SemiAnalysis now rates GCP a Gold managed-cluster provider while Google is simultaneously scaling external TPU sales and multibillion-dollar capacity commitments, showing the cloud and accelerator platform is becoming commercially credible rather than remaining an internal-only technical asset.

CoreWeave’s operating-moat thesis materially strengthens but remains 4/5: SemiAnalysis still rates it the industry’s leading Platinum neocloud, with best-in-class reliability and unusually deep hardware/software operations, while its debt and cost of capital increasingly push growth toward lower-margin, financeable bare-metal contracts.

Nebius enters the tracker at 5/5 because SemiAnalysis now rates it a Platinum neocloud and the default provider for frontier AI labs, combining premium managed-cluster execution, early next-generation GPU deployment and unusually strong revenue-per-MW economics with a credible multi-gigawatt expansion path.

Oracle enters the tracker at 4/5 because SemiAnalysis now rates OCI a Gold GPU-cloud provider, expects it to post the largest relative hyperscaler growth in 2027, and finds strong day-one GB300 cluster execution, while uneven AMD operations and concentrated capital commitments keep conviction below the leaders.

TeRAM’s 3D-SRAM thesis materially strengthens at 4/5 because SemiAnalysis has now publicly argued that decode-expert workloads can gain dramatically from SRAM-resident weights and that fast, large 3D memory will be decisive for long-context inference efficiency—technical support that closely matches the architecture SemiAnalysis Capital recently backed.

Nvidia’s platform thesis re-strengthens to 5/5 because Rubin’s first verified agentic-inference results show a large next-generation performance/TCO and power-efficiency lead while Nvidia’s day-zero model support continues to demonstrate the practical CUDA/software moat that competitors still struggle to match.

AMD’s AI-accelerator thesis weakens back to 3/5 because recent selective MI355X TCO wins have not yet generalized into a robust production-software moat: on the new DeepSeekV4.1 Flash release AMD lagged Nvidia on day-zero support and remained dramatically worse on current performance per dollar.

SK Hynix’s HBM thesis partially re-strengthens because SemiAnalysis’s new 4-hi analysis argues shorter HBM stacks can improve dollar-per-bandwidth, stacking yield and supplier profitability per scarce DRAM wafer, offsetting part of the prior margin concern even though Hynix’s company-specific HBM4 leadership and Nvidia bargaining-power issues remain.

Bloom’s behind-the-meter AI-power thesis materially re-strengthens: despite reciprocating engines remaining the broad share leader, Bloom now owns essentially all tracked fuel-cell bookings and is winning large deployments because its low-NOx, labor-light, vertically integrated fuel-cell model can clear permitting and execution bottlenecks that combustion equipment cannot.

SemiAnalysis’s reciprocating-engine thesis materially strengthens: behind-the-meter AI power has moved from early deployments to a 75GW firm-order market, recips continue gaining share as turbine slots push beyond 2030, and Caterpillar is nearly tripling large-engine output while 24/7 prime-power duty creates a recurring service cycle.

GE Vernova remains a strong turbine-scarcity beneficiary, but SemiAnalysis’s current BTM work redirects the thesis: factory slots now extend past 2030 and secondary-market premiums confirm exceptional scarcity pricing, while faster-growing recip and fuel-cell suppliers are capturing more of the marginal datacenter-specific volume.

Dylan Patel is making a direct high-conviction bet that AI inference is becoming memory-bound enough for Positron’s memory-first architecture to create a major alternative accelerator platform by using commodity LPDDR5X to bypass HBM and advanced-packaging bottlenecks.

OpenAI’s 5/5 thesis strengthens again: model-driven serving optimization is directly lowering inference cost while its custom-ASIC program has asymmetric strategic value—successful Jalapeño raises revenue per MW, while even failure can extract substantial Nvidia financing and backstops.

Anthropic’s thesis materially strengthens: SemiAnalysis expects Anthropic and OpenAI to absorb roughly half of incremental global AI compute by end-2027 and potentially 70–80% by 2028 because frontier-lab revenue per MW lets them economically outbid other buyers.

Broadcom’s custom-AI-silicon thesis materially strengthens because OpenAI’s first-generation Jalapeño ASIC, built with Broadcom, is already a credible high-volume Rubin-class inference competitor, validating Broadcom’s ability to monetize frontier labs’ shift from merchant GPUs toward custom accelerators.

Cerebras materially strengthens its ultra-low-latency inference proposition with CS-4, nearly doubling per-user token speed at roughly similar customer TCO while improving rack manufacturability and enabling heterogeneous disaggregated inference.

SemiAnalysis still believes SpaceX can scale AI compute toward 10GW by year-end 2027 and monetize scarce capacity at exceptional pricing, but its current published base case points to roughly $300B of ARR rather than the $500B figure previously captured in the ledger.

Vertiv is positioned to roughly double its revenue content per datacenter megawatt as AI builders shift from component purchases toward integrated modular power, cooling and facility platforms that materially shorten construction schedules.
ASML is entering a stronger multiyear wafer-fab-equipment upcycle, with improving visibility, pricing and installed-base economics creating upside to consensus revenue and likely long-term guidance.

Meta still has unusual advantages in data, talent, compute and distribution, but infrastructure politics and repeated hardware co-design failures materially reduce confidence that its enormous capex will translate efficiently into frontier-model and external-compute returns.
TSMC’s advanced-node capacity is becoming the central AI-silicon bottleneck, supporting exceptional utilization, customer dependence and pricing power.

a16z’s fal thesis strengthens into a Machine Age-relevant inference bet: multimodal generation can become a real-time computing workload when model post-training is co-designed with systems and hardware optimization, making the inference platform—not just the foundation model—a major performance and value layer.

rows.category: World Models / Spatial Intelligence / Robotics Simulation
rows.summary: a16z’s World Labs thesis materially strengthens as Atlas moves spatial intelligence from generative 3D toward a reusable world-model layer that can reconstruct, generate and simulate physical environments, making simulation and real-to-sim-to-real robotics a more credible scaling infrastructure for physical AI.

rows.partner: Raghu Raghuram; Sarah Wang; Shangda Xu; Stephenie Zhang
rows.summary: AI inference is becoming too heterogeneous and power-constrained for one-size-fits-all compute, creating a new infrastructure layer that dynamically maps each model, tool and inference stage to the processor and physical configuration that delivers the best latency, throughput and cost per watt.

rows.partner: Ben Horowitz; Martin Casado; Raghu Raghuram; David Ulevitch; David George
rows.summary: a16z is making a firm-level $1.1B bet that AI’s physical stack—from chips and memory through networking, data centers, robotics and electricity—must be rebuilt because demand is outrunning today’s supply chains and engineering limits.

Compute access is increasingly a project-finance bottleneck as well as a GPU bottleneck, and a vertically integrated neocloud that combines land, power, financing and cloud operations can unlock capacity for AI-native companies that hyperscaler-oriented infrastructure markets underserve.

a16z is making a high-conviction bet that specialized robotics and industrial AI can become the computing layer for the physical economy, with Atoms applying autonomy to making, moving and storing physical goods across food, mining and transport.

rows.partner: Guido Appenzeller; Raghu Raghuram; Jason Cui
rows.summary: AI data centers require a new networking control plane because multi-network GPU fabrics are too complex and too economically critical to manage with cloud-era tooling.
Motors and actuators are a strategic physical-AI bottleneck, and domestic manufacturing can become valuable as robotics and drones scale while U.S. OEMs reduce dependence on Chinese component supply.

The next major automation wave requires integrated models, dexterous hardware and deployment infrastructure designed together, because a large share of factory work is too variable for traditional industrial robots.

rows.partner: Raghu Raghuram; Shangda Xu; Guido Appenzeller
rows.summary: AI networking is becoming a defining bottleneck and could create a new major networking platform because existing switching products were designed for cloud traffic rather than rapidly scaling distributed AI workloads.

The grid’s next bottleneck is power delivery and control, and software-defined solid-state transformers can become a new platform layer as AI data centers and distributed generation overwhelm passive legacy equipment.

rows.partner: Matt Bornstein; Guido Appenzeller; Raghu Raghuram
rows.summary: GPU scaling should continue, but ubiquitous intelligence also requires radically more efficient accelerator architectures, creating room for new hardware design points beyond general-purpose GPUs.
